analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and restores pre-2010 law.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the consumer financial watchdog died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, which created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and restore the law as it stood before that Act [S2][S3]. The Bureau is the federal agency that writes and enforces rules for credit cards, mortgages, payday loans, debt collection, and other consumer financial products, and it has returned billions of dollars to consumers from companies it penalized. Senator Cruz introduced the bill with eight Republican cosponsors [S4]; the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be banks, credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, debt collectors, credit reporting agencies, and other financial companies that the Bureau polices. Without the Bureau, they would face no dedicated federal regulator writing consumer finance rules or bringing enforcement actions, and companies penalized by the Bureau would keep money it has obtained for consumers. Individuals injured by financial practices would lose the single agency whose job is to take those complaints and cases.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the statute that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and revives the law as it existed before that Act [S2][S3].

Repealing the Act would eliminate the Bureau, its rulemaking authority over consumer financial products, and its enforcement actions against financial companies, leaving oversight of credit cards, mortgages, and loans to weaker or fragmented regulators [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who use credit cards, mortgages, auto loans, payday loans, and debt collection or credit reporting services would bear the cost: no dedicated agency would police those markets, consumers injured by illegal practices would have to rely on individual lawsuits or state agencies, and money the Bureau recovers from violators would stop flowing back to customers.

drawbacks.text: Supporters' good-faith argument is that the Bureau's structure is unaccountable: its director was historically removable only for cause and it is funded outside the normal congressional appropriations process, so critics say it wields major regulatory power without usual checks [S3].

The honest cost to the other side is that abolishing the Bureau entirely, rather than restructuring it, would remove the one federal agency dedicated to enforcing consumer financial rules and recovering money for harmed consumers, with no replacement in the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit would go to regulated financial firms in the form of removed oversight; its cost would fall on consumers, who would lose the agency that handles their complaints, writes market-wide rules, and returns money obtained from violators. The bill offered no replacement mechanism for consumer financial enforcement, so the trade-off runs almost entirely against ordinary users of credit.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took the bill up, so it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on May 6, 2019, with eight Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S4][S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber [S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau survives, and the financial companies hoping to see it abolished did not get their repeal. No senator ever had to vote on the record to eliminate the consumer watchdog.
